cmCourseInfo.description: Intended for students with no background in Mandarin or any Chinese dialect, this course provides an introduction to modern standard Chinese as a foreign/second language. The course consists of mandatory lectures and tutorials. Students study a minimum of 450 Chinese characters. Students must go through screening process conducted by the Department. See www.eas.utoronto.ca/languages/chinese for details.

cmCourseInfo.prerequisitesText: Students must go through screening process conducted by the Department. See https://www.eas.utoronto.ca/languages/chinese for details.

Students will learn 600 characters. Students must go through placement process conducted by the Department. See www.eas.utoronto.ca/languages/chinese for details.

cmCourseInfo.description: Examines how various histories of East Asia can be written by focusing on specific themes in the histories of China, Japan, and Korea to roughly 1600. Required of EAS specialists, majors, and minors.
cmCourseInfo.title: Premodern East Asia

cmCourseInfo.description: Examines how various histories of East Asia can be written by focusing on specific themes in the histories of China, Japan, and Korea from roughly 1600 to the Cold War. Required of EAS specialists, majors, and minors.
cmCourseInfo.title: Modern East Asia

cmCourseInfo.description: This course is designed to help students build communication skills in the Korean language. Through an integration of listening, speaking, reading and writing, it aims to provide a solid foundation in beginning-level Korean. This course assumes that students do not have any prior knowledge of Korean. Students must go through screening process conducted by the Department. See https://www.eas.utoronto.ca/languages/korean for details.
cmCourseInfo.title: Modern Standard Korean I
cmCourseInfo.prerequisitesText: Students must go through screening process conducted by the Department. See https://www.eas.utoronto.ca/languages/korean for details.

cmCourseInfo.description: This course is for students with no or a very limited background in Japanese. Not eligible for CR/NCR option.
cmCourseInfo.title: Modern Standard Japanese I-a
cmCourseInfo.prerequisitesText: Students must go through a screening process conducted by the Department. See https://www.eas.utoronto.ca/languages/japanese for details.

cmCourseInfo.description: This course, which is a continuation of EAS151H1, is for students with some background in the Japanese language. All students must go through a screening process conducted by the Department. See https://www.eas.utoronto.ca/languages/japanese for details. Not eligible for CR/NCR option.
cmCourseInfo.title: Modern Standard Japanese I-b
cmCourseInfo.prerequisitesText: EAS151H1 (minimum of 60%) or equivalent as determined by the placement process. Students who did not take the prerequisite in the same academic year must take the placement test.
cmCourseInfo.exclusionsText: EAS120Y1, EAS222Y0, LGGA81H3

courses.name: Consumption, Taste and Culture in East Asia

cmCourseInfo.description: This course explores the roles that consumption and taste play in personal and public lives in East Asia. Course focus may include the cultural histories of food, fashion, tourism, sports, or forms of audio and visual media. (No prior knowledge of East Asian languages or cultures is necessary.) Restricted to first-year students. Not eligible for CR/NCR option.
cmCourseInfo.title: Consumption, Taste and Culture in East Asia

cmCourseInfo.description: The term "world-making” is often used nowadays to refer to transmedia storytelling, or the creation of story-worlds across serial narratives in a range of entertainment media, such as novels, games, film series/franchises, television shows, comics, and webtoons. This course looks at the ways that media producers and fans, alike, engage with media worlds. More importantly, the course situates these media worlds within a broader conception of "world-making," namely, the geopolitical and economic configuration of modern East Asia. (No prior knowledge of East Asian languages or cultures is necessary.) Restricted to first-year students. Not eligible for CR/NCR option.
cmCourseInfo.title: Media Worlds and East Asia

cmCourseInfo.description: This course is a continuation of EAS100Y1. Students learn major grammatical structures which are not introduced in the first year and expand their vocabulary. Students who do not meet the prerequisite must go through a placement process conducted by the Department. See www.eas.utoronto.ca/languages/chinese for details.
cmCourseInfo.title: Modern Standard Chinese II
cmCourseInfo.prerequisitesText: EAS100Y1 (minimum grade 67%)/equivalent as determined by placement process.
cmCourseInfo.exclusionsText: EAS101Y1, EAS201H1, LGGB60H3, LGGB61H3, LGGB62H3, LGGB63H3, CHI203H5, CHI204H5

courses.name: Modern Chinese II for Students with Prior Background

cmCourseInfo.description: This course is a continuation of EAS101Y1. It focuses on development of students’ listening, speaking, reading, and writing skills at an intermediate low level. Students who do not meet the prerequisite must go through placement process conducted by the Department. See www.eas.utoronto.ca/languages/chinese for details.
cmCourseInfo.title: Modern Chinese II for Students with Prior Background
cmCourseInfo.prerequisitesText: EAS101Y1 (minimum 67%)/equivalent as determined by placement process.
cmCourseInfo.exclusionsText: EAS200Y1, LGGB60H3, LGGB61H3, LGGB62H3, LGGB63H3, CHI203H5, CHI204H5

cmCourseInfo.description: Required of EAS specialists and majors, this course introduces various approaches, theories, and methodologies for the study of East Asian societies and cultures. As the course serves as a foundation for upper-level EAS courses, it should be taken as early as possible, preferably in the second year.
cmCourseInfo.title: Approaches to East Asia

cmCourseInfo.description: As a continuation of EAS110Y1, this course is designed to help students improve their skills in the Korean language. Students in this course are expected to perform basic communicative functions, read and write paragraph-level texts, and conjugate verbs/adjectives accurately. Students who do not meet the prerequisite must go through placement process conducted by the Department. See https://www.eas.utoronto.ca/languages/korean for details.
cmCourseInfo.title: Modern Standard Korean II
cmCourseInfo.prerequisitesText:
EAS110Y1 (63% minimum)/ equivalent as determined by the Korean placement interview.
Students who do not meet the prerequisite must go through placement process conducted by the Department. See https://www.eas.utoronto.ca/languages/korean for details.

courses.name: Accelerated Modern Standard Korean I & II

cmCourseInfo.description: Covering both EAS110Y1 and EAS210Y1, the course is ideal for self-motivated students who enjoy fast-paced language learning, students with a passion for Korean films and television, students with some listening and speaking skills from prior study or family background, and students taking the full four-year course series. Successful completion of the course fulfils the prerequisite for EAS310Y1. Students must go through screening process conducted by the Department. See www.eas.utoronto.ca/languages/korean for details.
cmCourseInfo.title: Accelerated Modern Standard Korean I & II
cmCourseInfo.prerequisitesText: Students must go through screening process conducted by the Department. See https://www.eas.utoronto.ca/languages/korean for details.

cmCourseInfo.description: As a continuation of EAS110Y1, this course is designed to help students increase their Korean communication skills at beginner high to intermediate low levels. It is ideal for self-motivated students who enjoy fast-paced language learning, and students who have built basic language skills from prior study. Successful completion of the course fulfils the prerequisite for EAS310Y1. Students who do not meet the prerequisite must go through placement process conducted by the Department. See www.eas.utoronto.ca/languages/korean for details.
cmCourseInfo.title: Accelerated Modern Standard Korean II
cmCourseInfo.prerequisitesText: EAS110Y1 (70% minimum)/Students who do not meet the prerequisite must go through placement process conducted by the Department.

cmCourseInfo.description: This course aims to strengthen Korean language learners’ literacy skills by developing reading fluency, comprehension, and critical analysis across diverse genres. Students will engage with authentic texts and practice reflective reading to expand vocabulary, deepen cultural understanding, and sharpen higher-order skills such as interpreting, summarizing, and evaluating. In addition, extensive reading activities, with books chosen by students according to their interests, proficiency levels, and instructor guidance, will foster confidence and independence as readers. By balancing cultural insight with critical engagement, the course supports advanced communication skills and complements oral communication classes. Lectures will be conducted in a mix of Korean and English to facilitate both acquisition and comprehension.
cmCourseInfo.title: Reading in Korean Across Genres
cmCourseInfo.prerequisitesText: EAS110Y1/ EAS211Y1/ LGGA10H3 and LGGA12H3/ a placement interview

courses.name: Cultural History of Food in East Asia

cmCourseInfo.description: This course introduces historical, literary, and anthropological issues related to the consumption of food and/or drink in East Asia. Through a wide variety of reading materials, it focuses on the relationships between food/drink consumption and commerce, religion, social regulation, medicine, and cultural identity, among others.
cmCourseInfo.title: Cultural History of Food & Drink in East Asia

cmCourseInfo.description: Pivoting on the recent and growing global prominence of Chinese science fiction, this course takes the history of science fiction in China as an entry point into studying the literary history of a global genre. The course surveys the Euro-American origin of science fiction, introduces students to the earliest Chinese sci-fi and fantasy literatures, and guides students through major science fiction works produced by modern and contemporary Chinese authors, while cultivating critical skills of close reading and distant reading. The course aims to rekindle the joy of reading and thinking in the literature classroom while demonstrating how science fiction offers fresh perspectives on technology, culture and the future.
cmCourseInfo.title: Chinese Science Fiction

courses.name: Perceptions of China in Japanese Literature

cmCourseInfo.description: Lectures on Japanese literary negotiations with China, the Chinese and Chineseness, ranging from celebration of shared cultural practices and aestheticization of China to nativist resistance to Chinese cultural hegemony. Required readings are available in English translation, including Tale of Genji, Tale of Middle-Councillor Hamamatsu (medieval romance), Haku Rakuten (No Play), Battles of Coxinga (Kabuki play), Three-Cornered World (by Soseki), and Wild Goose (by Ogai).
cmCourseInfo.title: Perceptions of China in Japanese Literature

cmCourseInfo.description: A historical introduction to Chinese philosophy, covering selected figures and texts from the Warring States period through the Qīng dynasty. Schools of thought covered include Confucianism, Mohism, Daoism, Legalism, “Profound Learning,” Neo-Confucianism, and “Evidential Learning.” Texts and thinkers include the Confucian Analects, Mòzǐ, Mèngzǐ, Xúnzǐ, Dàodéjīng, Zhuāngzǐ, Hán Fēi, Guō Xiàng, Zhū Xī, Wáng Yángmíng, and Dài Zhèn.
cmCourseInfo.title: Introduction to Chinese Philosophy

cmCourseInfo.description: A survey of the history of Japan from about 1600 until the disintegration of the Tokugawa regime in the mid-19th century. Uses a wide range of translated primary Japanese texts to illuminate the emergence of cultural forms and their conjunction with social, economic, religious, and political trends.
cmCourseInfo.title: Early Modern Japanese History

courses.name: Sinophone Cinemas: Revolution of the Sensible World

cmCourseInfo.description: This course is an introduction to the cinematic avant-garde movements that follow the end of the first Cold War across the Sinophone world, specifically China, Hong Kong, and Taiwan. Taking up the legacies of the Cold War, we examine specific film histories in each region and situate the New Wave movements of the past four decades in a vast terrain that is shaped by the narratives of war, nationalism, colonialism, economic integration, urbanization, among others.
cmCourseInfo.title: Sinophone Cinemas: Revolution of the Sensible World

courses.name: Aesthetics and Politics in 20th Century Korea

cmCourseInfo.description: This lecture course examines key questions and texts in the history of literature from the Korean peninsula during the twentieth century, exploring how aesthetic form refracted the experiences of colonialism, division, and the formation of opposing nation-states.
cmCourseInfo.title: Aesthetics and Politics in 20th Century Korea

cmCourseInfo.description: This course is an advanced beginners' level Japanese language course, which is designed for those who have completed EAS152H1 or EAS120Y1 or EAS121H1 with a minimum grade of 67%. All students must go through a screening process conducted by the Department. See https://www.eas.utoronto.ca/languages/japanese for details.
cmCourseInfo.title: Modern Standard Japanese II-a
cmCourseInfo.prerequisitesText: EAS152H1 or EAS120Y1 or EAS121H1 (minimum of 67%), or equivalent as determined by the placement process. Students who did not take the prerequisite in the preceding academic year must take the placement test.

cmCourseInfo.description: This course, which is a continuation of EAS252H1, is for students who have a good foundation of lower beginners' grammar, vocabulary and kanji knowledge and have not yet acquired the proficiency required to take EAS350Y1 (previously EAS320Y1). All students must go through a screening process conducted by the Department. See https://www.eas.utoronto.ca/languages/japanese for details.
cmCourseInfo.title: Modern Standard Japanese II-b
cmCourseInfo.prerequisitesText: EAS252H1 (minimum of 60%) or equivalent as determined by the placement process. Students who did not take the prerequisite in the same academic year must take the placement test.
cmCourseInfo.exclusionsText: EAS220Y1, EAS221H1, EAS223Y0

cmCourseInfo.description: A survey of major works in premodern Chinese literature, including poetry, essays, and short narratives from the pre-Qin through Tang eras (11th century BCE - 10th century CE).
cmCourseInfo.title: Chinese Literature (Pre-Qin to Tang)

cmCourseInfo.description: This course examines canonical literary works written in classical and sinitic Japanese (bungo and kanbun), including poetry, narrative, and theatre, produced from the Nara Period to the Edo Period (roughly 8th to 19th Centuries), with an emphasis on rhetoric, media, performance, reception history, canon formation and gender relations. Themes include: orality and literacy; masculine and feminine discourses; image and text; poetry and narrative; (auto)biography and fiction; intertextuality and authorship; the supernatural and realistic; establishment and resistance; and the centre and periphery. All readings will be in English.
cmCourseInfo.title: Classical Japanese Literature

cmCourseInfo.description: This course examines the tumultuous events of 19th-century Korea – from peasant uprisings to gunboat diplomacy and from the decline of slavery to the economy’s integration into global capitalism – together with the ways these events have been subjected to the changing and contentious interpretations of historians.
cmCourseInfo.title: Narratives of 19th-Century Korea

cmCourseInfo.description: Through various forms of popular culture in the 20th century, this course explores the cultural contexts and social trajectories of China, Japan and Korea. Forms of popular culture studied include art, visual culture, consumer habits, foodways, advertising, music, and fashion.
cmCourseInfo.title: Popular Culture in East Asia

cmCourseInfo.description: This course offers an interdisciplinary treatment of the Chinese people’s protracted struggle to transform the world's oldest empire and to create a revolutionary society, with a special focus on the myriad revolutions, uprisings, and protests that had radically remade the country’s social fabric in the tumultuous twentieth century. First-person accounts, classic and revisionist scholarly works, and literary and visual materials will be used to examine China’s multifaceted transformations both chronologically and thematically, in their socioeconomic, cultural, political, and global contexts.
cmCourseInfo.title: Revolutions in Modern China

cmCourseInfo.description: This course introduces environmental issues that are important to East Asia. Or better put, it examines the role East Asia plays in the global environmental crisis. We engage both the factual and humanities' dimensions of Climate Change, biodiversity loss, and other urgent environmental crises.
cmCourseInfo.title: Environment and East Asia

cmCourseInfo.description: A study of Chinese, Japanese or Korean culture, history and/or literature. Content depends on the instructor. When offered, the course will have a subtitle that describes its content.
cmCourseInfo.title: Topics in East Asian Studies

cmCourseInfo.description: A study of Chinese, Japanese or Korean culture, history and/or literature. Content depends on the instructor. When offered, the course will have a subtitle that describes its content.
cmCourseInfo.title: Topics in East Asian Studies

cmCourseInfo.description: This high intermediate-level course is a continuation of EAS200Y1. Students learn to read short texts which deal with cultural and social topics, compose paragraph-length essays, and converse in social situations which require exchanges of basic information and generate interpretations. Students who do not meet the prerequisite must go through placement process conducted by the Department. See www.eas.utoronto.ca/languages/chinese for details.
cmCourseInfo.title: Modern Standard Chinese III
cmCourseInfo.prerequisitesText: EAS200Y1 (minimum 70%)/ equivalent as determined by placement process.
cmCourseInfo.exclusionsText: LGGC60H3, LGGC61H3, LGGB62H3, LGGB63H3, LGGC62H3, LGGC63H3, CHI303H5, CHI304H5

courses.name: Modern Standard Chinese III for Students with Prior Background

cmCourseInfo.description: This course is the equivalent of EAS300Y1 with an accelerated learning pace. It is for students who have either completed successfully EAS201H1 or reached the intermediate-mid level in speaking, listening, reading and writing by prior study.
cmCourseInfo.title: Modern Standard Chinese III for Students with Prior Background
cmCourseInfo.prerequisitesText: EAS201H1 (minimum 70%)/ equivalent as determined by placement process.
cmCourseInfo.exclusionsText: EAS300Y1, LGGC60H3, LGGC61H3, LGGB62H3, LGGB63H3, CHI303H5, CHI304H5

cmCourseInfo.description: As a continuation of EAS210Y1 and EAS211Y1, this course is designed to help students improve their Korean proficiency at the intermediate level. The class focuses not only on oral fluency and grammar but also on reading comprehension. Students who do not meet the prerequisite must go through placement process conducted by Department. See www.eas.utoronto.ca/languages/korean for details.
cmCourseInfo.title: Modern Standard Korean III
cmCourseInfo.prerequisitesText: EAS210Y1 (67%)/EAS211Y1 (67%)/EAS212H1 (67%)/equivalent as determined by placement process

cmCourseInfo.description: This course examines the historical development of Japanese monsters, from roughly the 7th - 8th centuries to modern times. We focus on how the changing understanding of monsters in society has embodied certain fissures in Japanese culture, especially with regard to gender and class.
cmCourseInfo.title: A History of Japanese Monsters

courses.name: Precarious Island: Taiwan in the World

cmCourseInfo.description: This course is a thematic survey of twentieth- and twenty-first-century Taiwanese literature and culture, set in archipelagoes and oceans caught in the global history of colonialism and imperialism, the twentieth century wars, the unfinished Cold War, environmental crisis, and AI chip war.
cmCourseInfo.title: Precarious Island: Taiwan in the World

cmCourseInfo.description: Beginning with the Chinese Exclusion Acts, the Asian presence in North America has often been considered a serious social menace. This course explores the Asian/North American response to the past and present "Yellow Peril" constituted as a gendered, sexualized, classed, and racialized epistemological and affective structure of knowledge.
cmCourseInfo.title: The "Yellow Peril": Past & Present

cmCourseInfo.description: This course examines contemporary Korean language through diverse media, including pop culture, news, drama, and film. Students analyze authentic dialogues, expressions, and cultural nuances to strengthen linguistic and pragmatic competence. Instruction emphasizes real-world intercultural communication in modern Korean media contexts.
cmCourseInfo.title: Korean Language in Media
cmCourseInfo.prerequisitesText: EAS210Y1/ EAS211Y1/ EAS212H1. If you do not meet the prerequisites, a placement interview is required.

cmCourseInfo.description: Explores modern Japanese literature, with special attention given to literature's relation to the nation. Students explore how literature transforms throughout Japanese modernity and how its meaning and effects function to simultaneously solidify and fracture national identity.
cmCourseInfo.title: Japanese Fiction and the Nation
cmCourseInfo.prerequisitesText: EAS105H1 and at least one (0.5 credit) course in literature

courses.name: Science, Technology and Society in Modern China

cmCourseInfo.description: Learn to understand modern China from an understudied yet important perspective: the development of science and technology since the establishment of People’s Republic in 1949. Science and technology have played crucial parts in China’s political, economical, social, and cultural transformations. Drawing from anthropological, social, and historical studies of science, we examine, among other topics, science and nation-building, biopolitics, technocracy, and scientists’ self-fashioning at the junction of Communist reign and global capitalism. Students also learn key concepts of science studies.
cmCourseInfo.title: Science, Technology and Society in Modern China

courses.name: Cross-Cultural History of Scents and Aromatics

cmCourseInfo.description: This course surveys the importance of smell as a form of knowledge and source of history, and explores the use of aromatics in medicine, food, ritual, and personal fragrance, along with their role as a global commodity in East Asia and beyond. Students will read a variety of medieval and early modern texts about aromatics as well as more recent studies on olfaction.
cmCourseInfo.title: Cross-Cultural History of Scents and Aromatics

courses.name: Gift, Plunder, and Exchange: Japan and World History

cmCourseInfo.description: This course critically re-evaluates the history and historiography of Japanese capitalism, imperialism/colonialism, and world-empire through the lens of three, distinct “modes of exchange”: gift, plunder, and commodity exchange. Inspired by Kojin Karatani’s The Structure of World History: From Modes of Production to Modes of Exchange (2014), this course explores the emancipatory politics inherent in the critical analysis of modes of exchange, and takes up historical cases from Japan, Hokkaido, Okinawa, Taiwan, Korea, China, and the “Greater East Asian Co-Prosperity Sphere.”
cmCourseInfo.title: Gift, Plunder, and Exchange: Japan and World History

cmCourseInfo.description: This is a lower intermediate level course for those who have completed EAS253H1 or EAS220Y1 or EAS221H1 with a minimum grade of 70%. All students must go through a screening process conducted by the Department. See https://www.eas.utoronto.ca/languages/japanese for details.
cmCourseInfo.title: Modern Standard Japanese III
cmCourseInfo.prerequisitesText: EAS253H1 and EAS220Y1 or EAS221H1 (minimum of 70%), or equivalent as determined by the placement process. Students who did not take the prerequisite in the preceding academic year must take the placement test.

courses.name: The Art and Politics of Video in Japan

cmCourseInfo.description: This course will study the history of Japanese video art, beginning in the 1960s (when the Sony Corporation released the first portable video cameras) leading to the contemporary moment in which recording devices (phones, surveillance cameras, computers) and new distribution models (the Internet, public projections) abound. Video art is neither cinema nor television, and its early history is marked by some of the most radical artistic and political experiments in the history of modern Japan. This course will focus on the aesthetics and politics of experimental video with an eye on its global flows and Japan’s central role in its development.
cmCourseInfo.title: The Art and Politics of Video in Japan

courses.name: China's Cultural Revolution: History and Memory

cmCourseInfo.description: No understanding of contemporary China is possible without understanding the ramifications of the Great Proletarian Cultural Revolution (1966-1976). This course considers this tumultuous episode as a field of historical research and conceptual inquiry. This course critically examines a wide variety of sources, including scholarly accounts, official documents, personal memoirs, oral histories, and literary works.
cmCourseInfo.title: China's Cultural Revolution: History and Memory

cmCourseInfo.description: The course examines the cultural practice of nature in China’s past and present, focusing on literary, artistic, spiritual, ethical, political, and scientific aspects of human-nature relation. Through scholarly works and primary sources, the course inquires into the cultural politics of human-nature entanglements.
cmCourseInfo.title: Culture of Nature in China

cmCourseInfo.description: This course investigates cinema's border-crossing modes of production, reception, and circulation, to uncover the ways in which the study of cinema enriches current theories and approaches to the transnational. Films and sites to be explored may include Asian co-productions (documentaries, feature films, shorts), transnational genre adaptations (e.g., The Ring/Ringu), and film festivals.
cmCourseInfo.title: Transnational East Asian Cinema

courses.name: Special Topics in East Asian Studies

cmCourseInfo.title: Special Topics in East Asian Studies

cmCourseInfo.description: This course aims to develop students’ abilities at an advanced level, with a focus on reading of fiction and non-fiction. Learners develop skills to better express emotions, describe complex scenes, and narrate events and stories. Students will improve their reading comprehension, strengthen writing skills, and advance speaking and listening skills through class discussions and oral presentations. Students who do not meet the prerequisite must go through placement process conducted by the Department. See www.eas.utoronto.ca/languages/chinese for details.
cmCourseInfo.title: Modern Standard Chinese IVa
cmCourseInfo.prerequisitesText: EAS300Y1/ EAS301H1 (minimum 70%)/ equivalent as determined by placement process

cmCourseInfo.description: Chinese for users whose proficiency level is at or beyond the highest level that is currently offered. Students develop linguistic skills and cultural competence to understand and research contemporary Chinese mass media, social media, and public discourse. The language of instruction is mostly Chinese – Mandarin.
cmCourseInfo.title: Chinese Language in Media
cmCourseInfo.prerequisitesText: EAS401H1/ EAS402H1/ EAS404H1 or self-identified advanced and near-native user of Chinese.

cmCourseInfo.description: This course aims to assist students with upgrading their language proficiency for specialized uses. It focuses on 1) business terms and expressions and 2) formal or semiformal discourse in business. The language of instruction is mostly Chinese – Mandarin.
cmCourseInfo.title: Business Chinese
cmCourseInfo.prerequisitesText: EAS401H1/ EAS402H1/ EAS403H1 or self-identified advanced and near-native user of Chinese

courses.name: Korean Language in the Workplace: Academic Internship

cmCourseInfo.description: In this course, students apply their Korean language skills in supervised academic internship placements across education, nonprofit, business, and cultural sectors. Through structured opportunities to use Korean in real-world workplace settings, students develop practical and sector-specific vocabulary, enhance intercultural communication skills, and build professional networks. Students complete 35-40 hours of placement work with a partnering organization, such as local high schools, community organizations, or Korean businesses, in addition to in-class seminars, readings, and assignments. They engage in workplace communication scenarios such as outreach, project coordination, teaching support, or cultural programming. Seminars emphasize goal-setting, professional skills, networking, teamwork, and critical reflection. Students produce a final capstone portfolio and presentation. This course integrates linguistic, professional, and intercultural competencies, culminating in a meaningful, high-impact experiential learning experience. Not eligible for CR/NCR.
cmCourseInfo.title: Korean Language in the Workplace: Academic Internship
cmCourseInfo.prerequisitesText: Completion of a 300-level Korean course with a minimum grade of A- OR any 400-level Korean language course. Short application and interview required.

cmCourseInfo.description: This course aims to assist students to upgrade their language proficiency for academic and professional purposes. It is ideal for students who seek career opportunities in Korea-related business or in higher education in Korean studies. Emphasis is on comprehension and composition of academic and business texts and preparation for Korean proficiency tests. Students who do not meet the prerequisite must go through placement process conducted by the Department. See www.utoronto.ca/languages/korean for details.
cmCourseInfo.title: Academic and Professional Korean
cmCourseInfo.prerequisitesText: EAS310Y1 (70% minimum)/equivalent as determined by placement process.

courses.name: Border as Method: Rethinking Frontiers in Asia

cmCourseInfo.description: This course rethinks the meaning of borders through literature, film, satellite imagery, museum, and other multimedia materials. Specifically, the course explores media representations of the histories and technologies of borders and maritime frontiers that shape our geospatial understanding of modern East and Southeast Asia. From mountains and rivers to thermal imaging, drone surveillance, and smart walls, borders are both physical and virtual, external and internalized. We will connect the DMZ in Korea, Jeju island, military bases in Okinawa, Taiwan’s offshore islands, Subic Bay in the Philippines, and the artificial islands in the South China Sea.
cmCourseInfo.title: Border as Method: Rethinking Frontiers in Asia

cmCourseInfo.description: This seminar provides an opportunity for in-depth reading and research into a specific topic in the cultural and intellectual history of Korea. Topics will vary each semester but may include colonial period print culture, the New Woman, the history of photography, and modernism.
cmCourseInfo.title: Korean Cultural Studies Seminar

cmCourseInfo.description: Land as part of the Earth is repeatedly reconfigured in China throughout the 20th century, first by the Reformists and pioneers of the New Culture, then by geoscientists and writers, as well as by economic planners and social thinkers of recent decades. This seminar provides a critical review of this multi-dimensional cultural and conceptual practice of land, as well as its possible role in the era of climate change.
cmCourseInfo.title: Chinese Cultural Studies Seminar: Land

courses.name: The Global Bildungsroman: Narratives of Development, Time, and Colonialism

cmCourseInfo.description: This course studies Bildungsroman, the story of an individual's coming of age, in the context of twentieth-century political, cultural, and social developments of imperialism, anti-colonialism, human rights discourse, and globalization. Our focus will be novels from the (post)colonial world and theoretical essays on the Bildungsroman form. The course aims to provide a model for rethinking literary history and genres within a global context. Authors may include Yi Kwangsu, Wu Zhouliu, Pramoedya Ananta Toer, Kang Younghill, Tsitsi Dangarembga, Camara Laye, amongst others.
cmCourseInfo.title: The Global Bildungsroman: Narratives of Development, Time, and Colonialism

cmCourseInfo.description: This seminar analyzes fascism in modern Japan: its ideology, theories, and practices. We define fascism as a symptom of imperialism, and also explore the critique of fascism in Japan by Japanese thinkers on the Left, such as Tosaka Jun, whose Japanese Ideology represents one of the most trenchant critiques of fascism.
cmCourseInfo.title: Fascism and Japan

cmCourseInfo.description: The course examines literature, film, and other cultural products that emerged in the aftermath of the earthquake and tsunami that hit Northeast Japan on March 11, 2011, as well as in the ensuing nuclear crisis at the Fukushima Tokyo Daiichi powerplant. We will explore the distinctive aesthetic forms and imaginaries that responded to such natural and human-made disasters.
cmCourseInfo.title: “Post-Fukushima” Literature and Culture
